questions.enonce_markdown:
The element Li, Be, B and C are successive elements in period (II) of the periodic table with first ionization energies 520, 903, 800 and 1085 kJ mol$^{-1}$ respectively.

(i) What is first ionization energy?

(ii) Explain why;

A: beryllium has a higher first IE than lithium.

B: the first ionization energy of boron is less than that of beryllium?

(iii) Complete the table below by giving the formula of the hydrides formed by the elements.

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F | Ne |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hydride | | | | | | | | |

(iv) Which two elements in a(iii) above form neutral hydrides *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) First ionisation energy:** the **energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms** of an element to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions: $\mathrm{X(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{X^+(g)} + e^-$ (units kJ mol$^{-1}$).

**(ii) Explanations.**

**A: Be (903) higher than Li (520).** Li is $1s^2\,2s^1$ and Be is $1s^2\,2s^2$: in both the electron removed is in the **2s subshell, in the same shell, shielded by the same $1s^2$ core**. Beryllium has a **greater nuclear charge** (+4 against +3), so the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electron is greater and the atomic radius is smaller. The outer electron is held more strongly and more energy is needed to remove it.

**B: B (800) lower than Be (903).** Boron is $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^1$: the electron removed is a **2p electron**, which is in a **higher-energy subshell, on average further from the nucleus** than the 2s electrons, and it is **shielded by the 2s electrons** (2s penetrates closer to the nucleus). These effects outweigh the extra nuclear charge, so the 2p electron of boron is removed more easily than a 2s electron of beryllium.

**(iii) Hydrides.**

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F | Ne |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hydride | $\mathrm{LiH}$ | $\mathrm{BeH_2}$ | $\mathrm{B_2H_6}$ (or $\mathrm{BH_3}$) | $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | $\mathrm{NH_3}$ | $\mathrm{H_2O}$ | $\mathrm{HF}$ | none (noble gas) |

**(iv) Neutral hydrides: carbon ($\mathrm{CH_4}$) and oxygen ($\mathrm{H_2O}$).** Methane and water are neutral to litmus. The others are not: $\mathrm{LiH}$ reacts with water to give alkaline $\mathrm{LiOH}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is basic, $\mathrm{HF}$ is acidic, and diborane is hydrolysed to give the weakly acidic boric acid.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The group IV elements of the periodic table are C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb.

(i) Complete the table below by giving the formulae of the oxides of the elements in the +4 oxidation state.

| Element | C | Si | Ge | Sn | Pb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oxide | | | | | |

(ii) Give the formula of one oxide in b(i) which is:

Amphoteric:

A green house gas:

(iii) The elements form tetrachlorides of general formula $\mathrm{XCl_4}$. Write the reaction of the tetrachloride of germanium with water. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

| Element | C | Si | Ge | Sn | Pb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oxide | $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ | $\mathrm{GeO_2}$ | $\mathrm{SnO_2}$ | $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ |

**(ii)** Amphoteric oxide: $\mathrm{SnO_2}$ (tin(IV) oxide; $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ and $\mathrm{GeO_2}$ are also amphoteric: they react with both acids and alkalis, for example $\mathrm{SnO_2} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2[Sn(OH)_6]}$). Greenhouse gas: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (carbon dioxide).

**(iii)** The tetrachlorides of Group IV (except $\mathrm{CCl_4}$) are **hydrolysed by water**: germanium(IV) chloride gives hydrated germanium(IV) oxide and fumes of hydrogen chloride:

$$\mathrm{GeCl_4(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{GeO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Transition metals characteristically form complex ions and show variable oxidation state in their compounds

(i) What is a transition metal?

(ii) Give one reason in each case to explain why transition metals.

A: form complexes

B: Show variable oxidation states *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A transition metal is a **d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell** (for example $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, $3d^9$, and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $3d^5$; scandium and zinc are d-block elements but not transition metals, since $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is $3d^0$ and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is $3d^{10}$).

**(ii) A: Why they form complexes.** Their ions are **small and highly charged (high charge density)** and have **vacant, low-energy d orbitals** (together with 4s and 4p) that can **accept lone pairs of electrons from ligands** to form dative (coordinate) covalent bonds.

**B: Why they show variable oxidation states.** The **3d and 4s subshells are very close in energy**, so a variable number of electrons (the 4s and some or all of the 3d electrons) can be lost or used in bonding, with successive ionisation energies rising only gradually (for example $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$; manganese from $+2$ to $+7$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The complex compound $\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5BrSO_4}$ exhibits isomerism

(i) What type of isomerism does the compound exhibit?

(ii) Give the structural formulae of the isomers *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The compound shows **ionisation isomerism**: the two isomers have the same formula but give different ions in solution because the bromide and sulphate ions exchange places between the inside of the complex ion (ligand) and the outside (counter-ion).

**(ii) Structural formulae** (cobalt is $+3$ and six-coordinate, octahedral, in both):

- $\mathbf{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}$: pentaamminebromocobalt(III) sulphate; Br is a ligand and $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is the free ion, so it gives a white precipitate of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ with $\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq)}$ and no precipitate with $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}$.
- $\mathbf{[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Br}$: pentaamminesulphatocobalt(III) bromide; $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is a ligand and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ is the free ion, so it gives a cream precipitate of $\mathrm{AgBr}$ with $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}$ and no precipitate with $\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq)}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Give the shape of the complex $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2NCH_2CH_2NH_2)_2}]^{2+}$ *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **Square planar.** Each ethane-1,2-diamine ligand (en) is bidentate and donates two nitrogen lone pairs, so copper(II) ($3d^9$) is surrounded by four nitrogen atoms in a plane (coordination number 4): $[\mathrm{Cu(en)_2}]^{2+}$ is square planar. (In water, two water molecules can bind weakly above and below the plane, giving a tetragonally distorted octahedron, but the shape of the complex ion as written is square planar.)
